newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore looks underground for more land space.
newsitem.headline: Singapore looks underground for more land space.

text.p: Plans to build a multi-million dollar subterranean complex to make better use of scarce land in Singapore could result in the biggest such facility to be built in the region, The Straits Times said on Monday.
The newspaper said a geological survey, yet to be officially approved, has pinpointed several potential locations, such as Kent Ridge Park in the western part of the island.
The underground project would provide space for similar facilities to those above ground in nearby Science Park, the site for some of Singapore's large high-tech companies and laboratories.
Government officials told Reuters the multi-million dollar project was still in a study stage, and no projects were being tendered out yet for actual work.
But the Straits Times said one major underground cavern project was already underway in Bukit Timah, in northern Singapore.
Such underground projects intend to make more attractive use of space for commercial, industrial and recreational facilities.

Sandstone dug out can be sold as a building aggregate to offset the cost of construction, and caverns also use less energy, offer more security and pose less pollution to the environment, the newspaper said.

It said a geolological survey costing Singapore $2 million (US$1.43 million) has been commissioned to study potential areas for such projects, providing technical and cost evaluations for underground oil storage, power plants and sewage treatment works.
The world's largest underground facility currently lies 70 metres (78 yards) below Kansas City in the U.S., converted for use as warehouses, factories and offices.
